evidence.fitness: Nearest prior work: Whitt (1989) 'Planning queueing simulations' gives exactly this M/M/1 run-length planning from the asymptotic variance; Law & Kelton (2000) ch. 9 demonstrate naive-interval and batch-means coverage on M/M/1 delays at rho=0.9; Schmeiser (1982) the batch-count trade-off; modern practice is overlapping batch means (Meketon & Schmeiser 1984), spectral/Skart/N-Skart and ASAP3 sequential procedures (Steiger, Lada, Tafazzoli & Wilson), MSER warm-up deletion (White 1997), and in MCMC the sqrt(n) batch rule and ESS (Flegal & Jones 2010). Every result here is a correct reproduction of known material, not new; none of the modern estimators is compared. A researcher could use it as a clean, reproducible teaching baseline, but it does not advance a question and is not a PhD-level programme (not in research/PROGRAMMES.md).
evidence.domain: Against Law & Kelton ch. 9 and Alexopoulos & Seila (1998) practice: the variance formulas, Lindley recursion, stationary AR(1) start and t quantiles are textbook-correct. Departures a simulation analyst would flag: fixed b=30 with no batch-size selection or test of batch-mean independence (von Neumann / lag-1 test), so the phi=0.99 and rho=0.9 failures are shown but no rule to avoid them is given; warm-up is a fixed 1000-2000 jobs, no MSER or truncation method; no comparison with OBM, spectral or standardized-time-series estimators; the SLA rule uses a two-sided 95% half-width as a one-sided bound (a 97.5% upper bound), not stated.

defects.what: The batch-means interval, the paper's remedy, is effectively untested: dividing its half-width by sqrt(L) instead of sqrt(b) and changing t(29) from 2.045 to 1.96 both leave all 10 tests green; test_cis only asserts h < 0.01 on an alternating series.

No new result: Whitt (1989) already plans M/M/1 run lengths from this asymptotic variance and Law & Kelton ch. 9 show the same naive and batch-means coverage failures; no comparison with overlapping batch means, spectral, Skart/N-Skart, ASAP3 or a batch-size rule (sqrt(n), Flegal & Jones 2010), and no MSER warm-up. Below the research/CLAUDE.md PhD bar and not part of a programme.

Section 2 computes the naive interval on the un-burned prefix full[:n] and the batch interval on the burned suffix full[burn:], so the two coverages are on different data (initial bias is small here, but the comparison is confounded).

Formula check uses 100 batch means (14% SE) and all three estimates land 5-24% high; a regenerative estimator confirms the Daley formula to within 1.3%. The paper's 'tighter test' (item 5) compares mean half-width 0.236 to 0.233 ignoring the t/z and c4 factors (expected 0.241 if exact).
README says 8 tests; the suite runs 10 (test_figure.py added later). Runtime '~2 min' is 66 s.
batch_ci silently drops the last n mod b observations and raises a bare KeyError for any batch count whose df is not in the hard-coded T975 table; no validation of phi or rho in [0,1).
The SLA certification rule uses the two-sided 95% half-width as a one-sided upper bound (97.5% one-sided) without saying so.

verdict: A small, correct and honestly labelled reproduction of classical simulation output analysis. The run reproduces byte for byte. Every number I recomputed matches: the AR(1) variance from the closed form, ESS and coverage, the t table, the run lengths, and the M/M/1 asymptotic variance, which a regenerative estimator confirms to within 1.3%, far tighter than the subject's own check. An independent re-simulation of the SLA case agrees within 2 SE. It misses the bar on verification: the batch-means interval, the remedy the paper recommends, can have its half-width or t quantile broken with every test still green. Fitness and domain are 2 because nothing goes beyond Whitt (1989) and Law & Kelton ch. 9. No modern estimator (OBM, spectral, Skart, ASAP3, MSER) or batch-size rule is compared, so it is a sound teaching baseline, not PhD-level research.
